impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 applies differently to method claims reciting functional genus limitations for antibodies, and whether such broad method claims are adequately enabled when any member of the claimed genus would be effective for the recited treatment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method-of-treatment claims covering anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache, despite Eli Lilly's argument that the claims were not enabled under Amgen v. Sanofi. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding undermines medical innovation by sustaining overly broad functional genus claims and conflicts with Supreme Court enablement precedent.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims covering functional antibody genera may find it easier to enforce such patents, as the decision suggests enablement standards may be more permissive for method claims than for composition claims after Amgen v. Sanofi.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitor pharmaceutical and biotech companies face increased risk of being blocked by broad functional genus method claims, potentially chilling innovation in the biologics space and increasing litigation costs for companies developing competing antibody therapeutics.

impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether, under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2), a reference patent may claim the filing date of its provisional application as its effective prior art date without requiring that at least one claim of the non-provisional patent be supported by the provisional's written description, as previously required under pre-AIA law by Dynamic Drinkware.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination and remanded, taking up the important question of whether the Board's Penumbra framework—which holds that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis does not apply under AIA § 102—is correct. The resolution of this issue will determine when provisional applications can establish prior art dates under the AIA.
impacts.positiveImplications: If Dynamic Drinkware's more rigorous written description requirement is extended to AIA proceedings, patent owners will have a stronger defense against IPR petitions relying on provisional filing dates to establish prior art status.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patents in IPR may find it harder to use reference patents' provisional filing dates as prior art if stricter written description requirements apply, potentially reducing the effectiveness of inter partes review as a tool for invalidating competitor patents.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive patent licensee that shifted its business operations to enforcement activities had 'ceased its business operations' under the license agreement, triggering automatic termination, and whether the license conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient to confer standing to sue without joining the patent owner.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's shift to patent enforcement did not constitute ceasing business operations under the license agreement with Texas A&M University, and that the exclusive license conveyed all substantial rights in the patents, granting TexasLDPC standing to sue without joining the university. This clarifies when exclusive licensees can independently enforce patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees, including patent assertion entities, benefit from clearer standards confirming their ability to sue for infringement in their own name without joining the patent owner, providing greater flexibility in licensing structures and enforcement strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face increased exposure as patent assertion entities operating under exclusive licenses can more easily establish standing, even when the licensee's primary business activity is enforcement rather than commercialization of the patented technology.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a dispute over software developed under a licensing and services agreement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's post-trial reduction of the jury's breach of contract award, reinstating the original jury verdict. The decision affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and technology licensors benefit from the court's willingness to reinstate jury damage awards and require district courts to more carefully consider alternative damages models in trade secret cases, strengthening enforcement of IP rights in technology licensing relationships.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacements for licensed software face significant trade secret misappropriation risk, and the decision signals that courts should be more receptive to plaintiff damages theories, potentially increasing exposure in technology licensing disputes.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the eligibility determination for some asserted patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement, and affirmed the damages award. The decision provides important guidance on how Alice step-two analysis applies to communications technology patents that improve data transmission capacity using mathematical optimization techniques.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies holding patents on signal processing and communications improvements benefit from the court's affirmance that certain technically-implemented claims survive Section 101 challenges, reinforcing that applied mathematical innovations in communications standards can be patent-eligible.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing industry communications standards (such as ATSC 3.0) face continued patent infringement risk, as the decision confirms that patents on constellation designs embedded in standards can be enforced and support significant damages awards.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess en banc framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences between designs rather than overall similarity, and whether claim construction involving functionality in design patents presents factual questions for the jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing in a design patent infringement case, with significant internal disagreement. Chief Judge Moore dissented, arguing that the Egyptian Goddess framework has been misapplied to improperly focus on differences rather than overall similarity, enabling premature summary judgment. The concurrence defended the existing framework as consistent with Supreme Court precedent.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the maintained framework that allows courts to resolve design patent infringement at summary judgment when designs are sufficiently distinct, reducing litigation costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent owners face continued risk that district courts will grant summary judgment of non-infringement based on design differences without fully examining prior art or submitting the overall similarity question to a jury, potentially weakening design patent protection.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a communications apparatus using a coupler with a transformer having a non-magnetic core to match impedance for signal transmission 'over air' are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even though the district court had found them indefinite.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness finding but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on the alternative ground of lack of enablement. The court held that while the claims were definite, they were not enabled because the specification did not enable the full scope of the claimed invention. This demonstrates the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds raised by the appellee.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to consider and affirm invalidity on alternative grounds, providing multiple avenues to challenge overly broad patent claims even when the district court's original basis for invalidity is reversed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that claims surviving one invalidity challenge may be invalidated on alternative grounds raised for the first time on appeal, underscoring the importance of ensuring claims are fully enabled across their entire scope.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's phrase 'survives the EPR,' or whether such a contract interpretation dispute must be heard by the regional circuit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a contract dispute arising from a patent litigation settlement agreement, finding that interpreting whether claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination was a state law contract question that did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question. The case was transferred to the Fifth Circuit.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties drafting patent settlement agreements benefit from clarity that disputes over settlement terms will be resolved under state contract law in regional circuits, potentially providing more predictable outcomes in familiar forums.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties who assumed the Federal Circuit would resolve disputes over patent-related settlement terms may face unexpected jurisdictional challenges and forum changes, adding cost and delay to post-settlement disputes.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in an antidumping sunset review within 15 days of initiation conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on the filing deadline.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's 15-day regulatory deadline for domestic interested parties to express willingness to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews is a permissible exercise of agency authority. The statute is silent on the deadline, and the regulation was the product of reasoned decisionmaking within delegated power.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers relying on antidumping duty orders benefit from clear procedural requirements, and Commerce retains flexibility to administer sunset reviews efficiently through reasonable regulatory deadlines.
impacts.negativeImplications: Domestic producers who miss the 15-day regulatory deadline risk losing antidumping protection, as the court upheld Commerce's authority to impose strict participation deadlines not expressly required by statute.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may rule on both improper venue under Rule 12(b)(3) and patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 via Rule 12(b)(6) in the same order, or whether a venue dismissal precludes reaching the merits of eligibility.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dual dismissal on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds, holding that a court is not precluded from addressing the merits of a Section 101 challenge even after finding venue improper. The '979 patent's e-commerce claims were found ineligible under Alice.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain merits-based rulings on patent eligibility even when venue is also improper, potentially providing broader preclusive effects against subsequent litigation in other venues.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities face greater risk that a single filing in an improper venue could result in both a venue dismissal and an adverse eligibility ruling that may affect subsequent enforcement efforts elsewhere.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court must provide sufficient detail in denying motions for Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 to permit meaningful appellate review, particularly where the patentee had notice of Section 101 problems from PTO rejections of related applications before filing suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded a denial of sanctions and attorney fees, holding that the district court's order lacked sufficient detail to permit meaningful review. The case involved a patentee that filed suit despite PTO § 101 rejections in related applications and a prior invalidation of a related patent, raising significant questions about exceptional case findings under § 285.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from heightened scrutiny of frivolous patent assertions, as the decision signals that district courts must thoroughly explain their reasoning when declining to award fees in cases with strong indicators of exceptionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk of fee-shifting and sanctions when asserting patents with known eligibility problems in related applications, as the Federal Circuit expects district courts to carefully address such circumstances.

impacts.caseName: Socket Solutions, LLC v. Import Global, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in granting a preliminary injunction barring the sale of an accused product based on patent infringement claims involving wall outlet cover technology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a preliminary injunction that had barred Import Global from manufacturing, selling, or importing its Neat Socket product. The decision addresses the standards for obtaining preliminary injunctive relief in patent cases, including claim construction and likelihood of success on the merits.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from rigorous appellate review of preliminary injunctions in patent cases, reducing the risk of being improperly excluded from the market before a full trial on the merits.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders seeking to enjoin competitors early in litigation face a higher bar, as the Federal Circuit demonstrated willingness to vacate preliminary injunctions where the lower court's analysis was insufficient.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the term 'internal diameter' in oil and gas wellbore tool patent claims, and whether the infringement and validity findings based on that construction were proper.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's infringement and validity determinations regarding patents for wellbore casing flotation devices used in the oil and gas industry. The case turned on claim construction of the term 'internal diameter,' which was central to both direct and induced infringement findings as well as damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies in the oil and gas services industry benefit from the Federal Circuit's careful scrutiny of claim construction in oilfield technology patents, ensuring that patent scope is properly defined before infringement liability attaches.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the oilfield technology space face the risk of having favorable trial outcomes vacated when claim construction is contested, requiring potentially costly retrials and prolonged litigation uncertainty.
